entries.title: Remaining leads from the survey of comparable agent orchestrators (Oct 2026)
entries.body:
Leads borrowed from comparable open-source agent orchestrators, surveyed in October 2026 (first imported from issue #671).
Nothing here is a commitment; these are leads to triage.
The orch checked each against the code on 2026-11-17: ideas lym has built or that proved moot are dropped,
partly built ones name only what is still open, and the eight most worth doing are notes of their own in this project.
Each bullet names its source project and the lym module it would touch.

## Plan validation and concurrency (quarry, Plan-Write, board)

- **Typed scope operations on cards** (foremerge): each scope carries an additive or breaking operation,
  and deterministic rules flag colliding pairs even when files do not overlap.
  Worth comparing against board labels and the alignment gate.
- **Symbol leases between concurrent tasks** (Fusion, ORCH): expiring leases on symbol keys serialize overlapping tasks,
  with a deterministic tie-break; lym keeps overlapping tasks apart by board labels.
- **Commit-time reservation guard** (ntm): a pre-commit hook refuses a commit touching what another task holds; needs leases first.
- **Criterion amendment ledger** (oh-my-claudecode): a card's acceptance text changes only through a recorded amendment in weft.

## Review (burler, Bouncer)

- **Quorum of differently-angled judges** (ccswarm): lym fans out lenses but has no quorum vote for high-risk segments.
  Since 2026-11-19 a run's parent orch can be asked to see and veto each Code-Review round and each drift judge ruling
  (`loom.code.review_ask_parent`, `drift.judge_ask_parent`); that is one extra judge, not a quorum.
- **Risk tier by changed paths** (yylo): globs over sensitive paths choose the review depth and the gate scope.

## Engine, recipes and governance (shed, tender, orch, board)

- **Cross-run quarantine** (Bernstein): a task that fails three times across runs is held, unless the failures were the host's.
- **Fork a run from a step with a tree snapshot** (Bernstein): `shed goto` moves the cursor but does not restore the warp tree.
- **Warm retry guarded by a workspace hash** (Bernstein): resume the native session only when the tree is unchanged.
  Partly met since `dfade5f9a`: a run agent whose session a crash, reboot or killed pane ended resumes it (engines with a `SessionResumer`, so not Codex);
  no tree hash guards that resume, and a retry after a timeout or a finished run still starts fresh.
  Since `f1311f21d` a row gate also replaces a cold gate fixer that a machine stop or a killed pane interrupted,
  resuming its session where shuttle can; no tree hash guards that either.
- **Evidence reuse by input identity** (yylo): verify is skipped on the same tree; a changed review prompt could rerun only the review.
- **Guidance at the next step boundary** (Conductor): a queue of operator guidance for the next producer's prompt.
  Partly met since 2026-11-19: `loom.notify_parent_on` mails the run's parent when a named row is reached,
  so the parent can brief that row's agent as it starts; there is still no queue of guidance lym itself folds into the prompt.
- **Batched operator questions with recorded assumptions** (Spec Kit `/clarify`, Conductor): Discussion-Write asks at most a few ranked questions,
  each with a recommended answer, and records unanswered ones as assumptions.
  Since 2026-11-19 a run's autonomous agents put their questions to the run's parent orch, not to the operator in their pane.
  Discussion asks in its pane only when `loom.discussion.interactive` is `true`, which is off by default and forced off by autonomy mode (`30ed1ee58`),
  so this lead concerns an interactive Discussion only.
- **Rate-limit wait**: the orch watcher wakes the orch after a usage reset; tender itself schedules no resume.
- **Standing goals and scheduled routines** (ORCH, CAO, Fusion): periodic triage, dependency bumps or `selfreport` sweeps.

## Agent sessions (reed, shuttle)

- **Waiting-for-input signal** (agent-of-empires): shuttle has an awaiting-input state; screen heuristics still decide readiness and startup.
- **Reference status patterns and a paste pitfall** (CAO): compare its regexes and its tmux bracketed-paste note with shuttle's readiness and creel inject.
- **Context forecasting** (ntm): the orch cycles its context; Webster's Master and the loom driver do not, and nothing forecasts.
- **Staggered spawns** (ntm): space Webster forks and batten fan-out by learned rate limits.

## Observability (report, weft)

- **Hash-chained run journal** (Bernstein): a hash chain over producer outputs makes an archived run self-verifying.
- **Unverified-completion rate** (Bernstein): a `lym report` view of completions with no test or gate behind them.
- **Commit-to-record links** (AgentNote): weft links to warp by a `Warp-SHA:` trailer; a note or trailer on each warp commit could link back.
- **Run diff** (ccswarm): `lym report` comparing two archived runs' timelines and token use.
- **OpenTelemetry spans per producer** (Conductor).

## Operator attention (orch, dobby, reed)

- **Attention feed with acknowledgement states** (ntm): dobby's wait reminders have no seen, snoozed or acknowledged states.

## Discussion review (Discussion-Write, stencils, pattern)

- **Requirements-quality checklist** (Spec Kit `/checklist`): items with IDs the Discussion-review judge answers one by one.
- **Fixed analysis categories** (Kiro): inconsistency, ambiguity, conflicts, unstated assumptions and missing edge cases as named lenses.
- **PATTERN rules handed to reviewers** (Spec Kit constitution): its rules as numbered MUSTs in plan and code review prompts.
- **Glob-scoped steering** (Kiro): stencils pull per-area guidance chosen by the paths of a plan's glyphs.

entries.title: Name config keys as <module>.<path> in Go comments, and guard string literals for bare keys
entries.body:
After `config-keys-nested` nests the config keys by area, about 525 Go comment lines in about 199 files, plus single-word keys on top, still name a template key bare.
PATTERN-config-key-names asks that such a comment say `<module>.<path>`.

Sweep every Go comment and package doc that names a config key to its nested `<module>.<path>` form.
A comment-only change, no behaviour or user-visible text.
Deferred from T3 code review round 1, finding F1, to keep that run short.


## From issue #265

Imported from [issue #265](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/265).

## What happened

A code review finding asked for a repository-wide sweep of config key names written without their module, and no tool finds them.
A grep over the underscored template keys was the only practical method.
It missed single-word keys such as `engine` and `scoper`, and any key that ended a string literal, so messages were reported done while several were not.
Self-check forks caught the misses.

An earlier implementer had also found bare key names in messages and help texts outside its card's packages:
`gatecli`, `batcher`, `battencli`, `beamcli`, `webstercli`, `hibernatecli`, `reportcli`, `preflightshed`,
`weaverengine` (`ResolveLadder` and `settingRefusal`), `sheddriver/tackler.go`, `shedarbiter`, `burlerengine/fix.go` and `loomshed/plancontext.go`.
Some of these may have been fixed since.

## Why it is abnormal

A message or help text naming a key without its module can regress at any time, and nothing detects it mechanically.

## What to do

Add a guard test that scans Go string literals for a config template's key names written without their module.

Provenance: task `config-keys-nested`, notes `burler-code-r1.md`, `11-module-key-messages.md`.

entries.title: A landing queue gates several ready runs as one batch and lands them together
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-27)

Each landing ran its own landing gate under the parent lock, one after the other, so with many runs ready the gates queued in series.

## Seen again (2026-11-28)

With five runs ready at Finalize, each landing made every waiting run's lock-free gate stale:
the parent moved by real code, so each run in turn merged the new tip and gated tiers 0 to 2 again under the parent lock, 10 to 15 minutes each,
while the waiting runs' own lock-free gates competed with the holder for the same gate slots.
The operator released this entry ahead of the measurement of `landing-lock-only-for-land` on that ground (operator, 2026-11-28).

## Since (`d87a9ce24`, `landing-lock-only-for-land`)

`Finalize` now merges the parent's tip and gates the merged tree with no parent lock held, and takes the lock only to land.
Ready runs therefore gate side by side.
A run whose parent moved during its gate merges the new tip and gates again,
and after `landing.finalize_lost_races` lost races (default 2) it merges and gates under the lock.
Each ready run still pays for its own gate, plus one for each race it loses.

Since `5c985d926` (`finalize-owed-tips-gate`), this also holds when the parent is ahead of origin only by owed landing tips,
except for a landing that needs GitHub only because of GitHub's repository rules.
Before, every landing on such a parent lost all its races and gated under the lock.

## Idea

A landing queue in the manner of GitHub's merge queue, bors or Zuul:

- A run ready to land joins a queue for its parent branch instead of gating and taking the parent lock itself.
- The queue takes the waiting runs, say A, B and C, builds the tree parent + A + B + C and runs the landing gate once on it.
- A pass lands all of them together.
- A failure is bisected (parent + A + B, and so on): the runs that pass land, and the culprit goes back to its own run's fixer.
- A later step may gate the prefixes in parallel (parent + A, parent + A + B, parent + A + B + C) so a failure costs little time.

No drift: the batch is gated exactly as it lands.
It saves the most gate time when many runs land often, and it costs the most to build:
a queue service, batch merging, bisection on failure and fixer handling for the culprit.

entries.title: Autonomy takes in new GitHub issues and runs them, so findings do not wait for the operator
entries.body:
## Seen

Runs file their findings as GitHub issues on the hub repository, and runs and other agents file notes on the board, such as bugs.
Nobody takes either in unless the operator acts, so under autonomy they lie until morning.
The orch runs intake only when the operator asks (operator, 2026-11-28).

## Operator decision (2026-11-28): autonomy comes in levels of scope

What autonomy may start is a level of its own, beside how far it settles stops (project `self-healing-autonomy`):

1. First level: autonomy acts only on tasks that are already tasks and already released.
   It settles their stops and lands them, and starts no new work.
2. Next level, a fuller autonomy: the orch also picks up the notes that runs and other agents file on the board, and incoming issues,
   decides what to do with each, and may turn them into tasks and start them.

Turning a note or issue into a task is the risky step, since autonomy could start large work the operator would not approve.
Raddle splits are the example: their first draft is regularly reshaped by the operator, as project `self-healing-autonomy` went from eleven parts to five.

## Idea

An autonomy module that owns the second level:
watch the board for new notes and the hub repository for new issues, import the issues, bundle the work by package,
chain it against running and waiting tasks, start it as darn light, and report what it started.
It shares its home with the stop settling that project `self-healing-autonomy` builds.

## Open

- Whether this is lym code (dobby or a new module) or an orch procedure.
- What the second level never starts on its own; likely raddle splits, projects, features, and darn solid or wide.
- How the scope levels combine with `beam.autonomy`'s levels from `self-healing-autonomy`.

- Whether a desktop-bar button runs it.

entries.title: Measure how much landing-lock-only-for-land cut the wait for the parent lock
entries.body:
## Why

`landing-lock-only-for-land` (`d87a9ce24`) made Finalize merge and gate with no parent lock held, and take the lock only to land.
Whether ready runs now land without queuing is unmeasured.
On 2026-11-28 `reset-partial-commit-push` still showed 38 minutes at Finalize with no agent activity before it took the lock on `main`.
The answer decides whether the landing queue note `landing-queue` is still worth building.

Until `finalize-owed-tips-gate` (`5c985d926`, 2026-11-28), a landing on a parent that was ahead of origin only by owed landing tips
lost all of its `landing.finalize_lost_races` races and then merged and ran verify under the parent lock.
Figures from landings before that commit can therefore include this fault.

## What to measure

From the drive reports and gate run logs of landings already made, no new runs:

- For each landing, the time from Finalize's start to taking the parent lock, the time holding it, and the lost races (`landing.finalize_lost_races`).
- How often a run fell back to merging and gating under the lock.
- The same figures for the landings before `d87a9ce24`, for comparison.

Cap: the last 20 landings before `d87a9ce24` and the first 20 after `5c985d926`, on the prime of this hub.

## Seen

Find why a live beam orch reads as down: the liveness read, the strand's record in reed's state, or both.

entries.title: A dependent task plans ahead from its dependency's record and plan, and waits only to build
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-28)

A chain of tapestry tasks where B depends on A runs fully in series: B's Discussion and Plan wait until A has landed, though the plan writer is the slowest row.
The six serial parts of project `fabric-core` are the case at hand.

In Millhouse, which LoomYard grew from, the operator sped such chains up by hand, with success:

- Once A's discussion record was approved, B's Discussion started, told to build on everything A had decided.
- Plan writing for B likewise started before A was done, from A's record.
- When A had landed, B merged A's changes, and a small fixer read the code changes and updated B's discussion and plan for what had moved.
- Only then did B's builders start, so the builders were the only part that waited for A.

## Design (operator, 2026-11-28)

Only for the recipe that starts from a stored decision record: darn has no separate plan row to run ahead,
and a run with its Discussion still to run never plans ahead, so B always plans from a record already approved.

1. B depends on A.
2. When A's plan is approved, B is released.
3. B runs Discussion and Plan as usual, Plan Perch included, with A's record and plan as input.
4. After B's plan is approved, a new producer row waits for B's dependencies: B parks there until A has landed.
5. When A has landed, that row merges B's parent into B, bringing in A's change,
   and a fixer updates B's decision record and plan for what A's change brought.
   This stays small when A kept to its own plan.
6. B then goes on to Webster as today.

The merge in step 5 also brings in whatever else landed on the parent, not only A.
That is no new cost: Parent-Align already meets the same landings later today.
Running the chain in a beam of its own keeps the parent quiet, so the merge in step 5 brings in little beside A.

## Bounds

- The choice is made up front, before B plans ahead, never after: a plan written ahead and then thrown away is the waste to avoid.
  From A's record and plan, estimate how much of what B builds on A will change;
  when A is estimated to change too much of it, B does not plan ahead and waits as today.
- A run parked in the wait row of step 4 does nothing useful, so it must not hold one of `beam.max_runs`'s run places.
- Each link planned ahead of landed code adds error to the plans, so the cascade is kept short.
- Open: when B's plan counts as done for C to start.
  Proposed: only when B has passed step 5, so C plans from a plan re-aligned against A's landed code and the chain runs at most one link ahead.
- Not for now (operator, 2026-11-28).

entries.title: Jacquard, a recipe that runs the tapestry rows after Discussion and refuses an entry with no stored decision record
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-28)

The operator now seldom runs a full tapestry without a motif first.
A task raddle files from a Sketch already carries `discussed`, so its tapestry run skips Discussion;
which tapestry run does Discussion and which does not is read from a flag, not from the recipe named.

## Idea

A new recipe, `jacquard`, holds the tapestry rows after Discussion: Plan, Plan Perch, Webster, review and landing.
It runs only on an entry with a stored decision record, a task filed from a Sketch or a discussed entry, and refuses any other at start.
Raddle names jacquard for the parts it files from a Sketch where it names tapestry today.

## Tapestry stays (operator, 2026-11-28)

Tapestry stays a recipe, and it is made of motif followed by jacquard: one source for each part, never a copy of jacquard's rows in tapestry.
The operator can say "run jacquard" with no doubt about whether Discussion runs, and "run tapestry" for both.

## Name (operator, 2026-11-28)

The recipe is `jacquard` in code, config, verbs and records.
The operator calls it "jacq" in chat and text; the task adds `jacquard` to lym's glossary (`internal/heddleengine/glossary.md`)
and "jacq" to the nicknames in the repository's instructions, beside "Sketch" and "Merriam".

entries.title: Weaver gets a batch timeout of its own, names deviations in its summary, records gate spans and is tested on the paths its bench missed

## Why

The Weaver bench of 2026-11-27 (`docs/research/weaver/bench-2026-11-27/report.md`) found Weaver can replace Webster as tapestry's implementer,
but named four changes to make first (operator, 2026-11-28: fix them, then bench again).

## Changes

1. A Weaver attempt gets a timeout of its own, sized to a batch.
   Today an attempt runs under `shuttle.run_timeout_min` (30 minutes), which its gate waits and gate fixers count against;
   the bench's first calibration batch hit it with three of four cards committed, and the retry climbed to Opus.
2. Weaver's `summary.md` names each batch's deviations and departures, as Webster's summary does.

3. The Weaver row records `gate_spans` for the plan-level verify, as the Webster rows do.
4. Tests pin the paths the bench did not reach: a lost strand, a resume, a failed plan-level verify and the ladder's third rung.

entries.title: Bench Weaver against Webster again on the same three landed plans, both run side by side the same day
entries.body:
## Why

The bench of 2026-11-27 (`docs/research/weaver/bench-2026-11-27/report.md`) had only one plan where Weaver and Webster ran the same day,
so its quality and cost comparison is thin.
It is run again after Weaver's four named changes have landed (operator, 2026-11-28).

## Runs

Exactly six implementer runs and six reviews:

- The same three plans as the first bench: `board-viewer-server`, `launch-manifest-parity` and `gate-test-map-mode`, from the same base commits.
- Each plan once with Weaver on its default ladder and once with Webster on its default models, the two started together, the same day.
- One Burler round per result, as in the first bench: a `sonnet[medium]` reviewer with the code lens fan and the archived record and plan as the answer key.

Set up each run the way the first bench did, in a worktree pair of its own.

## Report

A new report beside the first one, with the same tables: wall time, gate time, fixer time, dollars, ladder and stops, verify, diff and review findings.
It checks that the four changes show: no attempt killed by the shuttle timeout, deviations in `summary.md`, and `gate_spans` on the Weaver rows.
It explains where Weaver's saving comes from, measured rather than guessed: cache reads per batch for Weaver against cache reads per fork for Webster.

entries.title: Shed gains a row that repeats or unfolds into rows from a list, so a producer such as Weaver runs one step per batch
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-28)

Weaver runs its batches in its own Go loop inside tapestry's implementer row, because Shed could not step through them:
a recipe is a fixed file of rows and edges, and a producer's `Yield` ends the driver's loop (Weaver's decision record, Q1).
About 15–20% of Weaver's production code, its stop and re-entry glue, part of its resume and its run lock, therefore repeats in concept what Shed does.
Review rounds are a loop too, and the plan-ahead wait row of `pipelined-chain-planning` is a dynamic row.

## Idea

Let a recipe hold a row that repeats while its producer asks for another pass, or that unfolds into rows from a list its producer writes, such as a plan's batches.
Each pass or unfolded row then gets Shed's own stops, re-entry, resume, history and arbiter, and Weaver shrinks to a thin producer per batch.

## Bounds (operator, 2026-11-28)

- Shed is a vital part of lym, and changing its logic this deep can have fatal consequences.
- So the change is designed first, through motif, before anything is built,
  and it only adds: every existing recipe, row and edge runs as today, and a recipe without the new row kind takes none of the new code paths.
- Weaver stays as it is until the new row kind has proven itself; moving Weaver onto it is a task of its own.

entries.title: Weaver runs each batch as a Shed row of the new kind and drops its own stop, re-entry, resume and lock code
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-28)

About 15–20% of Weaver's production code repeats in concept what Shed does: its stop and re-entry glue, part of its resume and its run lock.
It exists because Shed had no row that repeats or unfolds from a list.

## Idea

Once Shed has that row kind and it has proven itself, move Weaver onto it:
each batch becomes a pass or an unfolded row with Weaver as a thin producer,
and Weaver's own stop record, re-entry, in-row resume and run lock give way to Shed's.
The model ladder, batch partitioning, verify fixer, in-flight strand probing and reset stay Weaver's, since Shed has no counterpart for them.

## Bounds

- Weaver's behaviour seen from the run stays the same: the same batches, ladder, journal, summary and outcome.
- A bench against today's Weaver on the same plans checks it before Weaver's own loop is removed.

entries.title: Tapestry chains plan the next task while the one before still builds
entries.body:
## Aim (operator, 2026-11-28)

A chain of tapestry tasks runs fully in series today, though the plan writer is the slowest row.
Starting the next task's planning before the one before has finished building gains more than parallel batches inside one plan,
which a card-graph study found buys about 1.6x at best (`docs/research/webster/parallel-batches-2026-10-17/report.md`).

## Parts

1. A recipe, `jacquard`, that runs the tapestry rows after Discussion and starts only from a stored decision record.
2. Plan-ahead on that recipe: a dependent task plans from its dependency's record and plan, parks before building, re-aligns after the dependency lands, then builds.

## Aim (operator, 2026-11-28)

The implementer row spends much of its time in gate runs: card gates, batch gates, the plan-level verify and the slot waits between them.
This project cuts how often and how widely the implementers gate, where project `test-speed` makes the tests themselves faster.

## Parts

1. A measurement of where the implementer rows' gate time goes now.
2. Cuts filed from its report, one task per lever the operator picks.

entries.title: Measure where Webster and Weaver rows spend their gate time since the card gate took in dependent packages
entries.body:
## Why

`docs/research/webster/webster-time-2026-11-08.md` named five levers worth 15 to 23 min of an 86 min Webster row, the largest the guard step in every card gate.
The Weaver bench of 2026-11-27 (`docs/research/weaver/bench-2026-11-27/report.md`) then found gate tier time per row 2.2 times its recorded figure,
the same day `a69580709` made the card gate also run the packages that depend on a card's packages.
Neither cause is measured, so the cuts would rest on guesses.

## What to measure

Read recorded data only: gate run records under the Bolt checkout's `.lym/gate/runs`, implementer state and row history, and the archived runs' records.
Start no run, agent, bench or gate call.

Take every Webster and Weaver implementer row that ended between 2026-11-20 and the task's start, split at `a69580709`'s landing.
For each, split the row's time into agent work, card gates, batch gates, plan-level verify, gate fixers and gate-slot waits.
Within the card gates, give the time of each step of the tier commands, the guard step and the dependent-package scope included.

## Report

A report under `docs/research/webster/` with those tables, before and after `a69580709`,
and for each of the 2026-11-08 levers whether it still holds and what it would save now.
Add any new lever the records show, and rank all of them by minutes saved per row.

entries.title: Plan and build become recipes of their own, so a planned task waits for its dependencies with no run held
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-28)

Motif already runs Discussion as a recipe of its own: it runs, stores its record on the entry and lands.
Plan and the implementer are rows inside tapestry, so a task planned ahead would have to park a run until its dependencies land.

## Idea

Split tapestry into three recipes, each run as its own cycle:

- X, motif: Discussion; stores the decision record in Bolt, since one record is often split into several tasks.
- Y, plan: Plan and Plan Perch for one task.
- Z, build: starts with a row that updates the plan for what landed since Y, then the implementer, review and landing.

A full run is X, Y, Z. One X often gives several Y, and each Y gives exactly one Z.

## Y and Z share one pair (operator, 2026-11-28)

- When Y ends, its task turns into a Z task with the same slug, so Z gets the same task branch and the same weft branch.
- The plan stays where it is written, in the pair's weft `_lym/plan`; it is never copied to Bolt, which would clutter it.
- Batten skips Worktree-Teardown when a Y run ends, so the local pair stays standing until Z starts in it.
- Nothing Z needs is trusted to origin: the pair is kept locally, since origin can be lost.
- A Y run ends with no run held: Z waits through the dobby's existing dependency wait, with no parked run and no wait row.

## Bounds

- One entry carries the task through X, Y and Z, its stage shown on the board, so the operator follows one entry and not three.
- Plan-ahead's bounds hold: Y of a dependent task runs only from an approved plan, and the choice to plan ahead is made up front.
- A standing pair with no run holds disk only, never a run place.
